A drop shot is a deceptive badminton technique that involves hitting the shuttlecock gently, making it fall just over the net before it lands on the floor. This can confuse the opponent, forcing them to rush forward to take the shuttlecock.

3. Clear:
A clear is a defensive badminton technique that involves hitting the shuttlecock high and deep into the opponent's backcourt. This can give the player more time to retrieve the shuttlecock.

4. Drive:

4. It promotes sustainable living: Composting is an eco-friendly way of living as it promotes sustainable living. By reusing waste products, one can reduce the carbon footprint.

1. Get a compost bin: You'll need a small compost bin with a lid to store your kitchen waste.

2. Choose a location: Find a spot on your balcony that is easily accessible and gets some sunlight.

3. Begin to collect kitchen waste: Collect kitchen waste, such as fruit and vegetable peels, eggshells, coffee grounds, tea bags, and stale bread. Avoid adding meat, bones, and dairy products as they can attract pests and produce a foul smell.

4. Add the waste to the bin: After collecting kitchen waste, add it to the compost bin. It's a good idea to layer green organic waste (such as fruit and vegetable scraps) with brown organic waste (such as dry leaves or shredded newspaper).

5. Mix the compost: Turn the compost regularly to ensure the waste is decomposing properly. If the compost is too wet, add more brown organic waste, such as dry leaves, and if it's too dry, add more green organic waste.

6. Harvest the compost: After a few weeks, the compost should be ready to use. You can use it to fertilize your plants or add it to your balcony garden soil.

content:Speaker assistant says: Here are a few suggestions to make piano practice more enjoyable for your child:

2. Encourage creativity: Along with the regular practice, encourage your child to be creative with the piano. Let them experiment with their own compositions, and give them the freedom to play songs or pieces they enjoy.

3. Break up the practice session: Instead of making your child practice for a long stretch of time, break it up into shorter sessions throughout the day. This way, they won't feel overwhelmed, and they will have time to rest and recharge.

4. Offer rewards: Offer your child small rewards for reaching certain milestones or goals. These rewards can be as simple as a sticker or a favorite snack.

content:Speaker user says: A stroke victim's newfound love of painting helped her reclaim strength and self-confidence.
The doughnuts come in all shapes and sizes. There’s an aerial view of a chocolate doughnut with colored sprinkles.
There’s a plump one with fruit jelly filling its center.
In one of the paintings, three Boston cream-esque doughnuts and an ivory-white cup of coffee hover on a blue background.
The paintings remind Lois Herring, 68, of her childhood and how her working-class mother would take her — on special occasions — to a doughnut shop three blocks from her Grand Rapids, Michigan, home.
After a tough stretch of years that included her husband’s death and a major stroke, those doughnuts are still providing her comfort and joy six decades later.
It’s also helped her physically.
Art therapy is a little-studied scientific area, but the limited research suggests it can be very effective.
Herring, who lives full-time at the Spectrum Health Rehab and Nursing Center on Fuller Avenue, didn’t pick up a paint brush in her first 63 years of life.
Now, she paints three times a week.
In addition to doughnuts, she paints dogs and cats. She even does commission work, painting portraits of hospital employees’ pets when they bring in photos for her to look at.
RaNae Couture, art coordinator for Spectrum Health’s expressive arts program, said she’s seen incredible progress from Herring as she’s fallen in love with painting.
“After she had a stroke, she was going through a very difficult time dealing with that and with changes in her life: living at Fuller, being away from her family, and all the different changes that come from living at a long-term care facility,” Couture said. “And with all the rehab that she needed, with medical issues from stroke, there was a lot of life-changing — I don’t want to use the word ‘issues’ — but a lot of challenges after her stroke. There’s a lot of anger and depression associated with strokes. A lot of depression, and depression often comes out as anger.
“At the time, it was also not easy for her to focus and concentrate, which it takes to do art,” Couture said. “But she gradually … improved over the years with her concentration and focus. And we’ve just kind of worked with her, just working in the art studio the way she wants to.
But over time, she has done more and more.
Others have taken notice. In May, Spectrum Health hosted an art show where it invited 400 people — staff, friends and family, among others — to view the work of the art therapy patients.
Herring sold 11 paintings at $30 apiece, mostly from her doughnut series.
Herring uses program volunteers to help her paint. She bounces ideas off them, watches YouTube videos with them and asks them questions about technique. In addition to doughnuts and dogs, she’s also branched out into flowers and landscapes.
Her speech has improved a lot in the past two years, she said, as she increases the volume and complexity of conversations with Couture, volunteers and other patients in the art therapy program.
She’s also grown more trusting, Couture said, as she develops relationships with people in the studio.
Herring said those relationships — and the paintings that come from those sessions — are her greatest joy.
Herring said she wishes she could show her husband the skills she’s acquired. In one painting, an adorable black-and-white dog stares earnestly off the canvas, flanked by two thick abstract lines and a soft red background.
The way the black and white are sharply split, and the two black dots for eyes, it slightly resembles a yin-and-yang symbol.

content:Speaker assistant says: Traveling with kids can be a challenging experience if you are not adequately prepared. However, with some planning, patience, and creativity, traveling with kids can be a fun and stress-free experience. Here are some tips to help you travel with kids.

1. Plan Ahead: Plan your trip in advance and get the whole family involved. Talk to your kids about what to expect on the trip, the different activities you will be doing, and the places you will be visiting.

2. Pack Strategically: When packing, pack snacks, water bottles, blankets, and other essentials that your kids will need during the trip. Also, bring along some entertainment options such as books, puzzles, and games to keep them occupied during long flights or car rides.

3. Choose the Right Accommodation: Look for family-friendly hotels or vacation rentals that offer amenities such as swimming pools, game rooms, and kids’ clubs. You can also opt for accommodations with kitchens to make meal times more convenient.

4. Keep it Simple: When traveling with kids, keep your itinerary simple and flexible. Don't pack too many activities into one day; allow plenty of time for rest and relaxation.

5. Be Mindful of Their Needs: Be mindful of your children’s needs and take breaks whenever they need them. Stop at rest areas during long car rides, and take breaks from sightseeing to let them run and play.

6. Involve Your Kids: Involve your kids in the trip planning and ask for their input on what activities they would like to do. This will create a sense of excitement and enable them to feel more engaged and enthusiastic.

7. Stay Safe: Make sure your kids are safe throughout the trip. Use child safety seats in rental cars, hold their hands when crossing the street, and use sunscreen to protect them from the sun.

Overall, traveling with kids can be an exciting and rewarding experience that creates lasting memories. With these tips, you can make traveling with your family stress-free and enjoyable. context:planning keywords: traveling, kids, planning, preparation, family, tips tags: travel, kids, tips

content:Speaker assistant says: Definitely! Jet lag can be a challenging experience, especially for kids. Here are some tips to help you manage jet lag:

1. Adjust your schedule: Try to adjust your family's sleep schedule a few days before departure. If you are traveling eastward, move your bedtime earlier, and if you are traveling westward, push it back later. 2. Stay hydrated: During your flight, make sure you and your kids stay hydrated by drinking plenty of water. Avoid caffeine and alcohol, which can disrupt sleep patterns. 3. Sleep on the plane: Encourage your kids to get some sleep on the plane so they can adjust to the new time zone. Bring along some comfortable travel pillows and blankets which can help them get comfortable and reduce any distractions. 4. Get outside: Once you arrive at your destination, try to get outside and soak up some natural light. Exposure to daylight helps reset the body clock which can help in reducing the effects of jet lag. 5. Keep Active: Try to keep your kids active and engaged, avoid long naps during the day, and keep your schedule light for the day after your arrival. Let your kids explore and discover the new place, which will help them get settled in faster. 6. Eat right: Meal times are another key factor in helping adjust to a new time zone. Make sure your family is eating healthy, well-balanced meals and snacks at the appropriate times in accordance with the new time zone.
